Whitman is a super smooth lefty with fastball and slider command who has a chance to blow up on a pro strength and conditioning program. After two years with just 5.2 total innings pitched at Purdue, Whitman transferred to Kent State for his junior year and posted a 2.60 ERA with 100 K and 29 BB in 81 IP. He throws quality fastball strikes despite a long arm swing, and his mechanical grace, especially at his size, and his command make him one of the better starting pitching prospects in the draft. Hitters can pick up Whitman's grip as his arm circles behind him, but then they don't see the ball again until it's right on top of them. The pacing of his delivery also catches hitters off guard, as Whitman accelerates his whole operation late in the process. His super quick arm stroke and ride/run life helps 92 play up. He could still stand to get stronger and might throw harder. The movement of his low-80s slider is tight and late, and he can land it for a strike or get a chase. His changeup isn't good or consistent, but we're talking about a guy who barely pitched in a competitive setting until 2023; if he had a good changeup, too, he'd be a top 20 pick. This is a great tip-of-the-iceberg prospect who should be in the late first round mix.

Lombard is the son of a former big leaguer of the same name and presents teams with a well-rounded collection of present tools and skills, as well as long-term physical projection that might lead some of those tools to be plus. An elegant and smooth defender, Lombard played all over the infield during pre-draft showcases because of the presence of other shortstops on regional teams' rosters. He has the range, feet, hands, and actions to develop as a shortstop in pro ball. Geared for oppo gap contact, Lombard also has relatively advanced feel to hit and routinely squares pitches up. His frame is still maturing and as he'll barely be 18 on draft day, Lombard is likely to grow into meaningful power as he ages; a lot of it had already begun to arrive in the spring of 2023. His defense and hit tool foundation, combined with the chance he grows into pop, make him a first round draft prospect and potential everyday infielder.

Explosive hitting hands and a projectable, athletic frame spearhead Houck's prospect profile. He has a top-hand dominant swing that generates considerable power across a short mechanical distance, and his feel to hit might improve as the two-sport star focuses solely on baseball (he's a Division I-quality QB prospect, too). Raw from a bat-to-ball standpoint and on defense, Houck is a high-upside dev project.

Taylor go off to a rough start in 2023 but righted the ship and hit a career-best 23 homers, ending his career at TCU slashing .318/.446/.604. While on the surface it seems like Taylor early-season swoon was a blip, he did have some swing-and-miss issues exposed in 2023. He lacks precise barrel feel and is extremely pull-oriented, creating a hole on the outer third of the zone. Taylor's hitting hands are still fairly explosive and he has average big league raw power right now, and room for more strength on his frame. He's a very rangy defender with a plus arm, and as long as he's getting to most of his power, he can have a 40-grade hit tool and still be an important big league contributor, if not an everyday third baseman. Taylor has more hit tool risk than is typical for a multi-year college performer, but should still go in the first round.

Pratt has lightning fast hitting hands and peppers both gaps with hard contact. His front side is a little stiff through the contact point, but Pratt rotates hard through the hips and hit the ball hard on the showcase circuit. He's likely to grow into more raw power as he fills out and should have a potent hit/power combination at maturity. Pratt makes some slick defensive plays at short for a prospect his size, especially when he's coming in on the grass, but his lateral range is probably a better long-term fit at third base.

Knoth has a lightning-fast arm that was only producing low-90s velocity throughout his showcase summer, but his drop-and-drive style delivery was incredibly athletic, his fastball was seasoned by riding life, and he was snapping off the best curveball in the class. Knoth's breaking ball is the Grim Reaper, an absolute yakker in the 78-80 mph range with huge downward break. He experienced a velocity boost in the spring of 2023 and moved from the early second round of the FanGraphs draft board into the first. Knoth doesn't have prototypical starter's size but he's a superlative on-mound athlete with mechanics that are as repeatable as they are electric. You can go nuts projecting on his changeup and a second breaking ball because of his arm speed and proclivity for spin. This is also a cold weather prospect who will still be 17 on draft day. Knoth's mix already looks like that of a premium reliever and he may just be scratching the surface of his ability.

As an underclassman, White was sitting in the low-90s, and had a snapdragon breaking ball and a great physical foundation on which to layer velocity. He unleashed even more heat at 2022 PG National (lots of 93-96 mph) and then shut things down for the bulk of showcase season, with scouts told it was a personal decision. This spring he came out looking more muscular and mature in the body and held mid-90s velocity throughout the spring, albeit under a very conservative workload. 
The components of White's delivery often get out of whack, and he's had issues throwing competitive strikes for much of his time as a high profile prospect. There's heightened risk here, not only because this is a teenage pitching prospect, but also because of White's below-average strike-throwing track record and because he hasn't quite proven he can hold mid-90s velo over anything close to a pro starter's slate of innings. His stuff is very similar to Jason Groome coming out, which is a reminder of how long prospects like this can take and that they sometimes don't get better. But lefties with this kind of arm strength or breaking ball quality are rare, even more so when they have both. There are three potential plus pitches here and a light year of mechanical consistency and strike-throwing development needed.

Even though he's one of the youngest prospects in the class, Nimmala is a ferocious rotator and is already able to generate considerable power because of the strength and quickness of his hitting hands. While aspects of his swing make him vulnerable to breaking balls on the outer third, Nimmala is able to create big power in a relatively short distance, and his swing isn't overly noisy or hard to maintain. He has a tendency to pull off of stuff bending away from him and struck out much more than expected during his senior spring, enough that he slid from the top third of the first round to the back based on his spring look. There are past examples of players who were suddenly K-prone as seniors and things still worked out (Nolan Gorman) and others when the strikeouts were a meaningful signal (Keoni Cavaco). At his size, Nimmala is more likely to end up at third base than he is to stay at shortstop, which means he has very little hit tool margin for error. The skill foundation here is still very enticing, and model-driven teams are likely to be on Nimmala because of his age and power. His upside hasn't changed but the perception about his likelihood to hit it has.

Wilken has plus-plus present raw power and has hit several balls harder than 115 mph during his career at Wake, and he generates that power with a comically simple swing. He's an extremely patient hitter who rarely chases, and most of Wilken's whiffs come against sliders that finish in the strike zone but that he simply can't reach. Overall his contact ability is a tad shy of average right now, and will probably trend down as he climbs the minors. But Wilken's selectivity and the lift in his swing help ensure that he'll get to all of his power in games, and his on-base skills help his offensive profile float enough that he could be an everyday third baseman. Wilken has big raw arm strength but his size and stiffness aren't a clean fit at third base in the big leagues, where he's measured against the Matt Chapmans and Nolan Arenados of the world. He'll need to work to stay as agile and mobile as possible to avoid a shift to first.

If you liked Craig Counsell's batting stance, then please enjoy Schanuel, whose hands start way above his head before they load in a pretty normal spot. It's common for hitters in college baseball to walk as much as they strike out, especially the good ones. Schanuel walked five times as often as he struck out in 2023, a cartoonish stat that helps illuminate his freaky feel to hit. His swing isn't sexy or explosive, he just finds a way to put the bat on the ball, and the natural uphill path of his cut helps him to hit for some power. He slugged .868 in 2023, which is more due to his consistency of contact than big power, and in fact, Schanuel has less raw pop than is typical of a first baseman. He is similar to Washington State alum Kyle Manzardo, a hit-tool driven first base prospect who is likely to hit enough to play a big league role, and maybe even make so much contact to buck trends and be a regular without huge power.

One can't help but malaprop Sykora into "Sequoia" because Travis is the size of a tree at 6-foot-6 and 220 pounds. He overpowers high school hitters with a downhill, upper-90s fastball and promising fosh changeup, which sometimes has nasty glove-side finish that can make you mistake it for his less consistent slider. He is apt to work his fastball at the top of the zone and mix in his secondaries to induce weaker, early-count contact, since his heater doesn't play as well in the middle and bottom of the zone. Sykora is already a giant and you just hope he can sustain his current level of arm strength in pro ball when faced with a starter's workload. If he can, he has a mid-rotation shot.

Eldridge has some of the best raw power projection in this draft. He already has plus raw pop and his gigantic frame gives him a shot to develop actual 80-grade raw power. At his projected size, he'll be a first base-only defender, putting a ton of pressure on Eldridge's hit tool to help him get to that power. There have been points during this draft process when one could consider Eldridge's hit tool a binary "no." He has vertical plate coverage from belt-level and below, dropping the bat head to turn on low pitches. He's vulnerable to fastballs on the outer third and doesn't track pitches consistently well, with his head often flying out ahead of contact. But Eldridge's swing isn't all that long and it only get easier for him to hit for power while staying short to the ball as he continues to get stronger. His swing has big uppercut loft that can make one confidant that when he does make contact, there will be lift and power. This still isn't a slam dunk profile, but a 35-plus homer outcome with a viable all-around offense at first base feels more likely now than it did seven months ago.

Cholowsky is a broad-shouldered, projectable shortstop with a multi-sport pedigree (he also played quarterback) and a baseball industry family (his dad played pro ball for nearly a decade in the minors and is now the Reds' Four Corners area scout, while his mom worked for the A's). He is the best defensive infielder in the 2023 draft class, with some of the slickest and flashiest defensive actions of any draft prospect since Francisco Lindor. He also posted surprisingly good bat-to-ball data on the showcase circuit (per Synergy, a 2-to-1 BIP-to-Whiff ratio across 362 pitches on film in 2022), but to the eye, his swing has a hole up around his hands. Most of Roch's contact is concentrated down-and-away from him, and he has impressive oppo power but he tends to inside out a lot of pitches he should pull. There are scouts who don't consider it a totally functional swing and there's risk Cholowsky's hit tool will prevent him from being a regular. But his defense is going to play at the big league level. He has a realistic utility infield floor with an everyday shortstop ceiling if he can get on top of pro fastballs.

Cholowsky is a broad-shouldered, projectable shortstop with a multi-sport pedigree (he also played quarterback) and a baseball industry family (his dad played pro ball for nearly a decade in the minors and is now the Reds' Four Corners area scout, while his mom worked for the A's). He is the best defensive infielder in the 2023 draft class, with some of the slickest and flashiest defensive actions of any draft prospect since Francisco Lindor. He also posted surprisingly good bat-to-ball data on the showcase circuit (per Synergy, a 2-to-1 BIP-to-Whiff ratio across 362 pitches on film in 2022), but to the eye, his swing has a hole up around his hands. Most of Roch's contact is concentrated down-and-away from him, and he has impressive oppo power but he tends to inside out a lot of pitches he should pull. There are scouts who don't consider it a totally functional swing and there's risk Cholowsky's hit tool will prevent him from being a regular. But his defense is going to play at the big league level. He has a realistic utility infield floor with an everyday shortstop ceiling if he can get on top of pro fastballs.

Gonzalez is a really tough evaluation because he performed for three years in the best conference in the country, but his swing and the way he plays defense are both atypical of a good big leaguer. After three seasons in the SEC, he wrapped his career with a .319/.427/.561 line and 30 more total walks than strikeouts. He shares many similarities with Bryson Stott: a left-handed hitting shortstop with a swing geared for low-ball contact and secondary skills that have allowed him to get by on defense despite his non-traditional style of throwing and middling range. Gonzalez's hands, actions, quick transfer, internal clock, and arm accuracy all make him a likely pro shortstop despite him lacking the traditional speed/range and max-effort arm of a big league shortstop. 
His level of statistical performance is rare and Gonzalez will barely be 21 on draft day, but his swing has a huge hole at the top of the zone that I fear will be exploited in pro ball. He hasn't become meaningfully stronger during his time at Ole Miss (in fact, he's regressed a little bit as an athlete) and often needs to wind up his whole body to swing hard, making mechanical concessions in the process. It's a more extreme version of the issues JJ Bleday would eventually be exposed by, and Bleday's SEC performance was also a red herring. There's volatility here. Gonzalez has some premium skills and baseball feel, and he was an exceptional college performer, but he doesn't pass the eye test. He's arguably young enough to improve upon his athleticism and strength as a pro, and I think he needs to do so if he's going to be more than a utilityman.

Viable shortstop defender, deft hitting hands from the left side, medium frame projection. Little bat wrap, hands work in a fairly explosive loop, front side bails at times. Some mechanical similarities to a lefty-hitting Keston Hiura. Smaller frame caps power projection, but also makes it more likely he stay at shortstop. This type of high school hitter usually goes in the comp round.

Matthews is one of the more polarizing prospects in the 2023 class, an unpolished collection of huge tools but mixed results. He's a well-built shortstop in the Ruben Gotay mold. His exit velos are as high as anyone's in the draft, including Dylan Crews, it's just that Matthews' feel to hit is not good. He didn't swing and miss excessively in college but the visual evaluation of his hit tool is not great, and Matthews especially struggles to get on top of high fastballs. He is a plus runner and will show you a max-effort plus arm, but Matthews is also a crude defender at short and not a lock to stay there. He's often slow to approach choppers in front of him and has to rush once he has the baseball, and his throwing accuracy is a mixed bag. He is as toolsy as any college player not going in the top 5 but is also incredibly risky for a college pick. The last time the Astros took a player whose scouting report read like this (huge tools college guy with hit tool risk) it was George Springer.

Groover has maybe the fastest hands in the entire draft. His swing isn't always connected but his hands rip through the zone in the blink of an eye, and his contact rates are shockingly good for how hard he swings. He is a very dangerous hitter to all fields and was only vulnerable to swings and misses when Groover would chase at NC State, which wasn't a ton. A transfer from UNC Charlotte, most aspects of his game still need polish, especially his defense. Groover often looks rushed and his throws frequently pull the first baseman off the bag, but his range and overall athleticism give him huge long-term ceiling with the glove. This is among the 2023 draft's more volatile and exciting prospects.

Born in Hawaii, Ahuna spent his first two college seasons at Kansas and had one of the hottest lines in all of 2022 college baseball, slashing .396/.479/.634 before transferring to Tennessee for his draft year. He wasn't eligible for the start of the season because Tennessee didn't handle the transfer process correctly, and it cast a pall on the rest of Ahuna's season, which was just fair. He struck out 73 times in 273 PA, twice as often as he walked. That's a 31% strikeout rate, a pretty serious red flag for a college hitter. Ahuna can spray pitches in the lower third of the zone to all fields, wielding doubles pop to both gaps, but Ahuna's bat path naturally cuts underneath high fastballs, which are increasingly common. He is a lock to stay at shortstop thanks to his hands, acrobatic actions, and huge arm, and he projects as an impact defender there, which is really the foundation of Ahuna's profile rather than his offense.

Martin had a breakout at the 2022 Area Codes, where he showed a sweet lefty stroke, a projectable frame, and the arm and actions to stay at short. His feel to hit is hard to evaluate due to a smaller showcase sample than is typical for a high-end infield prospect, but in short looks, it has been quite undercooked. Scouts were out in droves to watch Martin play travel ball in Arizona in January to try and drill down on the hit tool, which was going to be tough to evaluate against varsity arms in Colorado during the spring. He destroyed opposing Colorado high schoolers but that's not really telling. He's a very risky older infield prospect with a gorgeous swing.

A no-doubt shortstop with a plus-plus arm, Martin's middling feel to hit pulls his projection down into a medium-variance utility range. While his on-paper bat-to-ball performance is quite good, the visual evaluation of his feel to hit is not as strong, and Martin tends to swing underneath high fastballs. He's a fantastic shortstop defender with a great baseball frame, and he might end up running into enough power to outpace the utility projection despite resolve that his hit tool will be below average.

Sproat was the Mets' 2022 third rounder but didn't sign, so he'll be approaching his 23rd birthday as he enters pro ball, though age isn't an especially relevant variable in Sproat's case. A noisy, cross-bodied delivery has long driven big league relief projection for him, and he'd probably move quickly if 'penned proactively, but he's also held premium velocity as a starter for his entire career at Florida and has a deep repertoire. Sproat tends to sit 94-98 mph, and his sinking, upper-80s changeup is easily plus. He will occasionally show you a plus slider, too, but that pitch is less consistent. Sproat's fastball has tended to play below its raw velocity because of its sink and tail, but it's still a really nasty offering. Some teams have had success coaxing more sink and tail out of fastballs that are shaped like Sproat's is to the eye (Clay Holmes, Blake Treinen, maybe Brady Singer), so perhaps that's feasible here. That and/or a more consistent breaking ball are the keys to Sproat becoming a mid-rotation piece, while his floor feels like a setup man, especially if he throws harder in the bullpen.

Lasko is a physical, plus-running outfielder from Rutgers who hit .330/.428/.582 as a junior with more walks than strikeouts. He is short-levered and powerful, best at scooping low pitches and punishing breaking balls in the zone. He has a hole in his swing up and away, especially against big velo, but has some hit tool margin for error because of his ability in center field.

Ledbetter transferred to Mississippi State for his draft year after two stellar underclass seasons at Samford and hit .320/.452/.574 against the SEC in 2023. He's a tad vulnerable to up-and-away fastballs, but otherwise he is tough to beat in the strike zone, making adjustments to offspeed stuff in the middle of at-bats and striking hard contact to all fields. Ledbetter is more likely to be a core platoon option in the big leagues than an everyday player, but that type of bankable, quick-moving bat prospect tends to go from picks 30 to 45.

Floyd was a two-year starter at LSU whose stock exploded during the College World Series when he was topping out at 98 and bending in a nasty slider, which was suddenly much harder than his regular season sliders, often 87 mph or so. Floyd struckout 120 hitters in 90 innings as a junior using mostly his mid-90s fastball, which features big ride and misses bats in the zone. His slider tends to finish high but it's still good if it's as hard as his was late in the year. His arm speed helps him sell his changeup, which has good long-term projection because of his arm speed, and once in a blue moon Floyd will dump in an slower curveball. It's a starter's mix with starter's on-mound athleticism and what looked like a late uptick in stuff.

One of the more prominent pop-up guys in a draft that doesn't have all that many, Wolters began to show that his fastball velo was climbing during indoor workouts over the winter. This spring, he's been into the upper-90s with big life at the top of the zone. His physicality has changed dramatically compared to his showcase summer and not only is he stronger and throwing harder, but he seems to be more in control of his body and delivery now. Wolters has long had talent for spin and his low-80s slider rotates with plus rpm, showing more long-term potential than his current, average-looking offering. His arm action is long, so there isn't great changeup projection here, but Wolters has been able to make significant adjustments in a short period of time, an indication that he'll continue to do that. That could mean a splitter, or a second breaking ball, anything to give him a third pitch and round out his mix. He's atop a group of fastball/breaking ball high school pitchers in this FV tier because his arm strength is currently the best of the bunch.

You can make the argument that Peterson checks more scouting boxes than any other high school pitcher in this draft class except maybe a fully-operational Thomas White, and he entered the 2023 spring with a shot to emerge as a surefire first round prospect, but he wasn't throwing especially hard at NHSI and has had issues with breaking ball consistency this spring. He's young for the class, has a well-composed, high-waisted frame (that's closer to maxed than ideal, but still good), and his arm speed is sensational. He's parallel to the ground at layback, then creates vertical ride on his fastball by virtue of his hand position on release. His delivery already looks a lot like what teams like the Red Sox and Tigers try to get their pitching prospects to do, with a curt arm action, allowing for consistent release. Peterson's shapely mid-70s breaking ball has depth but sometimes lacks power and bite. He sells his changeup with his arm speed and, when things are clicking for him, his pitch mix is as advanced as any high schooler in this class. He was up to 97 mph toward the end of the high school season and is a high-upside prospect who should go in the comp or early second round, though that may not be high enough to keep him from heading to Florida.

This lanky righty from Jersey had a velo spike during his senior spring, and after sitting 90-93 mph last summer, he was touching 95-96 en route to state Player of the Year. 
Echavarria's breaking ball is nasty. His height and slot make it so that pitch is only ever descending; it doesn't float up out of his hand in an identifiable way. It's a plus weapon in the upper-70s and is going to be a big league out pitch. His changeup might be, too. He barely uses it right now, but Echavarria flashed plus mid-80s changeups on the showcase circuit in 2022. His fastball strikes are inconsistent and sometimes Echavarria spins on the heel of his front foot as it catches his motion, and he loses his line to the plate. It's pretty typical for pitchers with levers this long to scatter their fastballs at this age, and Echavarria's control is fine enough to project him as a starter. 
His frame is projectable on paper, but I'm inclined to round down on his fastball growth a little bit. This isn't a broadly built 6-foot-4 guy; he's 6-foot-1 with narrow, rounded shoulders. If he can simply maintain the low-to-mid-90s heat under a pro load of innings, that will be a win. Likely to get seven figures on draft day, Echavarria is a fairly typical prep arm with a good breaking ball and a shot to pitch in a big league rotation over time.

Every draft, there are a few high school pitchers who are sitting 90 mph the summer after their junior year, then have a huge uptick in arm strength the following spring. Ellwanger is one of those prospects. He sat 89-92 on the 2022 showcase circuit but, lanky and loose, his velocity exploded during his senior spring as he played his way into baseball shape after the basketball season. By June, he was comfortably in the mid-90s and had improved a 77-82 mph breaking ball that was often a limp, 30-grade curveball the prior summer. He punched out 17 hitters while sitting 93-97 in the 5A state semis. At a well-composed 6-foot-5, Ellwanger has a lot of long-term starter traits and the arrow is way up on two of his pitches. He needs to find a third distinct pitch, but he's among the more well-rounded high school pitchers now that he's suddenly throwing much harder.

He covers most of the plate, has power to both gaps, and if his offensive performance holds water against better pitching than Carico will see in the Atlantic 10, he might do enough on offense to be a primary catcher.

After he started just one game as a freshman, Honeyman had a breakout sophomore year when he hit .329/.402/.506 during the NCAA season and .289/.400/.530 on Cape Cod. He has fantastic breaking ball recognition, barrel control, and hitter's timing despite his sizable leg kick, and Honeyman can bend at the waist to hammer pitches on the outer edge of the zone. While he isn't a true burner, Honeyman's instincts and routes in center field are good enough to give him a shot to stay there for the long haul. He may not have a plus tool at peak, but Honeyman's game also doesn't have a hole and he seems likely to be an integral big league role player of some kind.

Watts-Brown was a high-profile transfer from Long Beach State who had a down 2023, walking a batter every other inning and posting an ERA around 5.00. His breaking ball quality is still so good, and Brown is such a smooth operator on the mound, that he still presents a dev-friendly foundation for a team in the second round. Watts-Brown's slider breaks late and his curveball has big time depth. Both of them are easily plus, while the rest of his skill set is below average. His delivery is more graceful than it is athletic and powerful, and scouts are split as to whether or not JWB is going to throw harder in pro ball. Pro teams don't consider Oklahoma State to be especially good at developing pitchers, so perhaps there's meat on the bone here, either in terms of coaxing more velo out of Watts-Brown by altering his mechanics or simply by helping him impart more effective movement on that pitch. He could be a no. 4 starter with an improved heater and more consistent release, and is more like a generic no. 5 if he can only find one of those things.

A very interesting late-bloomer prospect with a plus-plus pitcher's build and mid-90s arm strength, Lord transferred to UW from Division III Carleton College. He's had a nearly 10-tick velo bump since high school, and he's sitting 94, up to 97 with downhill cut. He has a construction crane build at 6-foot-3 with ultra-long levers. Lord's ridiculous shoulder mobility is evident on layback, and his breaking balls have big depth on occasion. His size, arm strength, natural breaking ball snap, capacity for movement, and the small school background make for a very exciting dev project. Lord is raw and had an ERA over 6.00, but his peripherals were pretty strong. He's undercooked enough that it's tough to project him as a starter, but this guy is just scratching the surface in every way and pitchers built like this tend to find feel later. There's big upside here, enough to take a risk early in the second round (yah yah).

A very interesting late-bloomer prospect with a plus-plus pitcher's build and mid-90s arm strength, Lord transferred to UW from Division III Carleton College. He's had a nearly 10-tick velo bump since high school, and he's sitting 94, up to 97 with downhill cut. He has a construction crane build at 6-foot-3 with ultra-long levers. Lord's ridiculous shoulder mobility is evident on layback, and his breaking balls have big depth on occasion. His size, arm strength, natural breaking ball snap, capacity for movement, and the small school background make for a very exciting dev project. Lord is raw and had an ERA over 6.00, but his peripherals were pretty strong. He's undercooked enough that it's tough to project him as a starter, but this guy is just scratching the surface in every way and pitchers built like this tend to find feel later. There's big upside here, enough to take a risk early in the second round (yah yah).

Johnson's slider could probably get big league hitters out right now. The upper-70s offering starts in the lefty batter's box and finishes over the plate, bending in at 75-80 mph with dastardly two-plane break. Johnson's fastball command and mechanics are not typical of a starting major league pitcher. He scatters his fastball locations, and has a nearly sidearm slot and a rather extreme head whack. Johnson also presents non-traditional body projection. He's always been quite big, and showed up to the 2023 Dream Series looking like an offensive tackle prospect. His body composition isn't bad, mind you — Johnson is yoked — he's just huge, and the only recent comparable physical entity upon entering pro baseball is Jasson Domínguez. There are many developmental hurdles for Johnson to clear if he's going to be a big league starter, from sustaining his peak velocity (at times he's sitting 97 mph, at others 92) to commanding his fastball, and developing command of a viable third pitch. Still, lefties with a slider like this tend to find their way into a late-inning bullpen role, and Johnson seems pretty likely to hold plus heat in such a role. He was shut down during the spring of 2023 with elbow tendinitis, perhaps making it more likely that he ends up at LSU.

A 6-foot-4 human trebuchet, Volchko has an extreme overhand slot that helps his fastball carry and his curveball dive. He is lanky and long and might yet throw harder as he matures. And more velocity has already started to arrive, as Volchko was 91-94 last summer but was peaking in the 97-98 mph range during the spring of 2023. His delivery is violent about the head and shoulders, and his hat often flies off his head during his release. His mechanics and inefficient style of pitching are bullpen indicators, but he might end up with two plus or better pitches and be a late-inning weapon even if that's true. He's committed to Stanford.

His athleticism and defensive footwork doesn't scream "slam dunk shortstop," but Stafura makes a fair number of acrobatic plays by virtue of his body control and feel for throwing accuracy; the latter enables him to hit the first baseman in the chest from odd and difficult platforms. Most importantly, Stafura can hit. Again, he isn't an explosive rotational athlete but he tracks pitches like a missle defense system and has a short, compact swing. Of the bat-driven infielders in the 2023 draft class, Stafura's bat-to-ball skill is about as good as a lot of the first round types, but he presents a less exciting athleticism/projection package.

Clemmey's high-octane delivery generates mid-90s velocity and an occasionally plus breaking ball. His cacophonous mechanics make for a very uncomfortable at-bat, especially for lefties, and also create a lot of relief risk. After he was parked in the 92-95 mph range on the showcase circuit and with Team USA, Clemmey will now show you 92-98 over the course of a full start. His NBA shooting guard frame and explosivity are signs that he is going to continue to throw hard, but probably not with touch-and-feel precision. Finding a more consistent breaking ball will be a huge key for Clemmey in pro ball (or at Vanderbilt, where he's committed) because his current 78-83 mph offering has inconsistent finish. There's exciting raw material here as Clemmey should at least become a good reliever with a monster fastball. His size and athleticism mean you can dream on more.

A power-armed righty with a high-effort delivery, Kuehler sits 93-95 mph as a starter but was up to 97-98 with Team USA over the summer of 2022. Despite a very short arm action, Kuehler's release varies in a way that impacts the shape and consistency of his breaking balls. His best curveballs have nasty vertical bite, while some of his sliders are 86-87 mph, and sometimes the two blend together and look hittable in the 80-82 mph range. Still, Kuehler is tough for hitters to square and he allowed just 111 hits in 157 innings the last two years. There's a chance for three plus pitches and late-inning relief here.

McGraw has had two elbow surgeries in the last half decade, missing his senior year of high school with a traditional TJ and his junior year of college with another elbow reconstruction, this time the internal brace procedure that's becoming more common. McGraw was generating buzz just before the season, with some scouts considering his stuff superior to Rhett Lowder's. He showed two above-average secondary pitches and mid-90s velo as a sophomore on Cape Cod and with Team USA, but his velo took a meaningful step forward just before he blew out for the second time, when McGraw was sitting 95-98. It's pretty important for all of that velocity to come back because McGraw's fastball plays down a little bit due to its shape. If it doesn't, then McGraw is more likely to be a reliever who leans a ton on his plus slider to get by. It has huge length and two-plane sweep, and hitters often swing inside it even when they identify slider out of hand because it just keeps bending and bending further away from them. McGraw also showed right-on-right changeup feel during the 2022 summer. There are three potential above-average pitches here, but the slider is the only one that's bankable as of draft time. There will come a point, probably early on Day Two of the draft, when McGraw's upside will trump the high-floored, vanilla college pitching alternatives in the mid/late-second round. This guy has mid-rotation upside when wholly intact and has missed two of the last five years with injury, perhaps scratching the surface of his pitchability.

Sanders had a down 2023 because of an injury to his knee and lower fibula, which caused him pain during the season even before he was shut down for most of May. It's quite a feat that Sanders only missed a month. This is likely a guy who'll be shut down after the draft so he can be completely healthy for next season. And healthy Sanders does a little bit of everything. He can work the angle of his fastball past hitters at the letters even though he doesn't throw incredibly hard, and both his changeup and slider are capable of missing bats when he executes location, which he tends to do. His fastball is pretty vulnerable in the strike zone, so Sanders doesn't have a great way to get ahead of hitters. He tends to use his changeup as an action pitch in the zone just to show a different look. Improving breaking ball demarcation (there are definitely two different pitches here, they just run together) as a pro might also help with this. The entire package presents a pretty low variance no. 4/5 starter look. He'd likely have gone toward the back of the first round if healthy, but he's now more likely to come off the board in the second.

An older high school prospect in the 2023 draft, Cupp's physicality leapt out ahead of his peers as an underclassman, but he has come back to the pack as the pre-draft process has unfolded. He still has plus bat-to-ball ability and lovely hitting hands, as well as the actions to develop as a shortstop (though he's not a lock to stay there). There's a chance his bat-to-ball skills carry him to an everyday big league role, though the context of his age relative to his peers casts some doubt on whether the feel to hit is actually special. Cupp's skills give him a utilityman's floor, though, and he feels like a probable big leaguer even if he isn't likely to have huge impact.

One of the lankiest, most projectable hitting prospects in the 2023 draft, if not tops by both measures, Gasparino has a big long-term power ceiling and a non-zero chance to stay in center field despite his size. It's hard to find major league comps for Gasparino because of his frame — at a broad-shouldered 6-foot-6, he's built more like a college basketball prospect. Hitters this big are almost always high-risk hit tool prospects because of their lever length, but Gasparino's body control at his age and size is encouraging. He glides from gap to gap, eating up ground with his big strides, and might be able to stay in center despite posting 45-grade run times from home to first (4.35, 4.66 with a turn, etc.), which would give his hit tool margin for error. He's among the highest-variance prospects in the 2023 class.

Mueth is a super loose Tanner Houck clone with an ideal pitcher's frame at a lanky 6-foot-6. His cross-bodied, low-slot delivery with a long arm swing creates uphill angle and tail on a fastball parked in the 92-94 mph range most of the time. Mueth has very little feel for location, and misses up and to his arm side a ton. He's raw in most facets but also has a chance to throw very hard over time and develop a fastball in the style of a righty Chris Sale, or Camilo Doval, or any extremely low-slot pitcher you can think of. His fastball and slider combination from this slot gives him a great chance to profile as a nasty reliever, at least, and given the right development, he could be an impact arm.

A power-hitting catching prospect who has hit in games on the showcase circuit, Helfrick has a shot to be a primary catcher because of his offense. He certainly looks the part of a pro athlete in the uniform at a sturdy 6-foot-2, and Helfrick is already capable of hitting for power to the right/center gap as well as to his pull side. Despite some breaking ball chase, Helfrick performed pretty well from a contact rate standpoint against his showcase peers. Most of his extra-base damage comes on pitches in a pretty narrow portion of the strike zone, mainly ones out away from him that he can get extended on. Helfrick's receiving is still pretty crude for his age, and his footwork and exchange need cleaning up, but these are common issues for a teenage catcher and Helfrick has above-average raw arm strength. The ingredients are here, they just need a lot of seasoning.

Tredwell has an absurd sophomore year in the bullpen with 62 K and 6 BB in 47 innings while throwing 85% fastballs. He had a two-tick bump in 2023 and began integrating more secondary pitches before he was shut down in April with back and rib injuries. Gigantic 6-foot-8 frames like this ordinarily create whiff-diluting downhill plane on the fastball, but Tredwell's does a ton of damage in the zone at 92-94 because he's generating nearly 21 inches of vertical break. He is not the sort of twitchy athlete who you expect to throw harder over time, but this fastball will play. Curveballs and sliders were more a part of Tredwell's 2023 formula; both are about average in quality and play down because he doesn't have a ton of experience throwing them. He hasn't proven he can eat a buffet's worth of innings yet, but his frame indicates it's possible. This is a high-volume backend starter prospect.

A "fastball-only" pitcher with close to 80% heater usage in 2023, which is actually down from 2022. Selected but unsigned by Baltimore in 2022 draft as draft-eligible sophomore. Back in 2023, he K'd 72 and walked just seven in 44.2 innings. Mid-90s fastball with incredible riding life, tons of swings and misses throughout the strike zone. It's a dominant offering that would be enough to spearhead a single-inning relief fit in pro ball. Has had no feel for finishing his slider/curveball in college and that desperately needs to be developed for him to be more than a middle relief option. How good of a second pitch he develops will dictate his future role. At best, he'll show you a slider in the 86-89 mph range with two-plane movement. Ideal pitcher's frame, three-quarters slot with bend at the elbow and north/south hand position that helps create ride.

Redshirt junior who was at Wake Tech and Catawba before Wilmington. Velo peaked during the postseason, where Banks was 96-99 mph at Regionals. Powerfully built 6-foot-3 with a short arm action that generates cut and ride on his fastball. Inconsistent fastball command and breaking ball shape. Sliders 85-87 with anything from cutter action to vertical drop, no consistency here, but promising amounts of movement. There's a right-tail outcome where Banks has a 70 fastball with upper-90s velo and maddening cut and a plus slider, the raw material for that is in here, but he needs a grade of command development to be anything at all. Middle relief is his most likely outcome.

Grice was an effective two-way player at Clemson and hit .288/.398/.560 during his career there, but when the Diamondbacks drafted him he was announced exclusively as a pitcher. Grice struck out 101 hitters in 78 innings as a junior, mostly because of his secondary pitch quality. Both Grice's upper-70s slider and mid-80s changeup can miss a bat, but his slider is especially nasty, bending in with tight two-plane movement. He's only sitting in the low-90s but if indeed Grice gives up hitting and focuses solely on pitching as a pro, there might be more in the tank in terms of stuff, across the board. He's a late-blooming starter prospect.

Maybe the best baseball build in the entire draft at a strapping 6-foot-6, built like young J.R. Richard but not nearly as explosive. Chance to layer big velo on through physical maturity and tweaks to his delivery. Flashes above-average breaking ball in the low-80s, but more consistently a 45 on the scale. No changeup feel. Built more like a big league starter than perhaps anyone else in the class and presents teams with a solid enough fastball/breaking ball foundation to build on.

Soto has a huge arm and was routinely in the mid-to-upper-90s on the showcase circuit and again during most of the spring of 2023. The track record of pitchers who are built like Soto and who throw with as much effort as he does isn't great, and I have apprehension about his fastball playability and long-term command projection. He is built like Red Sox righty Bryan Mata was at the same age and has a similar delivery, working with downhill sink and tail and a stiffer-than-average delivery. His sinker gives high school hitters fits, but big leaguers are going to hit it unless Soto accentuates its movement. He certainly has a starter's collection of secondary stuff, with a plus mid-80s slider and occasionally good changeup. He looks more like a sinker/sweeper reliever than a mid-rotation starter.

Bitonti has sizable power for a prospect who will still be several months shy of his 18th birthday when the draft arrives. His huge frame may cause a tumble down the defensive spectrum as he fills out (you're hoping for third base on the high end, an outfield corner in the middle, and 1B/DH on the low side), but he might hit enough to profile anyway. His bat-to-ball performance against elite peers waned as the 2022 summer went on and there is some hit tool risk here, but Bitonti's raw power projection, the lift in his swing, and the potential that his hit tool might polish up simply through maturation make him a notable early-round prospect. he reportedly wants $2.5 million to sign.

Taylor would have gone higher had he been healthy this spring, and given the dearth of college pitching in the draft he may have come close to the first round. Taylor was a 2022 Cape Cod breakout guy, he threw strikes there after working out of LSU's bullpen the spring prior. It looked like he'd seize a rotation spot along with Ty Floyd and Paul Skenes but instead his elbow ble wout just before the season and he needed Tommy John. Healthy Taylor works in the -with riding life and downhill angle, the latter detracts from the effectiveness of the pitch somewhat. He has a classic, upper-70s overhand curveball to go with it, as well as a slider Taylor barely throws. Taylor's longer arm action and somewhat violent delivery were bullpen indicators even before he got hurt. He has a non-zero shot to work in key spots if his peak velo returns post-rehab. His acquisition marks the second straight year the White Sox have drafted someone coming off of TJ.

Hitt is a lefty with above-average breaking stuff who had Tommy John in April. He's had walk issues all three years of college, and the feel for release is not especially sharp, weirdly pushing back onto his tippy toe as his delivery finishes over his front side. Of course, Hitt hasn't had a ton of college reps as a starter. He was in the bullpen as a freshman and only made eight starts in 2023 before his elbow blew out. Healthy Hitt brings low-90s heat with a little but of natural cut at times, not really missing bats at the top of the zone despite the vertical look of his slot. His breaking balls run the gamut from upper-80s cutters to mid-70s curveballs, all with bat-missing finish when located. He's a breakout candidate if, during rehab, his drafting club finds a way to help his fastball play a little better in the zone, and if they can make a solid average big league athlete (Hitt moves really well getting off the mound) with a typical frame and build find a way to have starter-quality command. He projects as a fifth starter, and fastball quality will be the most influential developmental variable.

Riemer does not swing and miss. You can count on your fingers the number of times he whiffed in 2022, as he seems to find a way to put the bat on the baseball no matter where it is in the strike zone. He isn't clubbing traditional extra-base power, but he is stinging the ball in a Steven Kwan-ish way that feels like it will translate to pro ball. Riemer has played shortstop at Wright State, but he isn't a realistic fit there in the pros due to a lack of arm strength, so there might have to be more power here if he can only play second base at the next level. If he ends up with an elite hit tool, though, he'll find a way to be a big league contributor.

Alderman's exit velos are absurd, the best in the entire 2023 draft class and scale-breaking when adjusted for his age. He hit a ball 118 this year and slugged .709 at Ole Miss. Alderman is trying to break the sound barrier when he swings, he puts every bit of his 250-pund frame into his cut. His breaking ball recognition is not great, and puts Alderman at risk of not getting to his power enough to profile at the bottom of the defensive spectrum. He has mostly played the outfielder corners to this point, and it's likely as Alderman ages that he won't be mobile enough to play defense anywhere. If that's the case then any sort of offensive flaw is going to be tough for him to overcome. He has a shot to be a middle of the order anchor but his overall contribution will be limited to that side of the ball.

George is a switch-hitting slash-and-dash high school prospect with elite speed. His wheels will enable him to play center field and could make him a plus defender out there. While his righty swing is more traditional looking, George's lefty cut relies on his speed to beat out infield hits, and most of his extra bases come via doubles grounded into the corners. Unless he can develop more pop from the left side, his ceiling is that of a traditional leadoff man or a modern nine hole hitter.

Looked meaningfully stronger during the spring of 2023, with fastball velos more often in the 93-95 mph range than the summer before. Upshot angle of heater gives it a shot to play at basically any velo in the 90s. Breaking ball quality is only okay, tends not to have nasty bite and depth but does have long break at times. Changeup is identifiable out of the hand right now, but he has feel for creating action on it. Relatively advanced fastball command and three-pitch foundation gives him a shot to start, breaking ball is more a potential big league weapon than a present one, and the cement is closer to dry on his frame than last summer.

He is a premium in-the-box athlete with a flexible and powerful lower half, as well as strong wrists that turn over through contact. At times he can look a little out of control, and a lot of that is because Keaschall swings a ton and finds himself off balance a lot of the time. He is also a 2B-only infielder because of his arm strength. He's a high-risk prospect because, if he doesn't hit enough to be an everyday second baseman, it's going to be tough for him to profile. Not yet 21 on draft day, Keaschell's age will put him in model-heavy teams' mix.

Horvath hit 42 bombs combined during his final two years at North Carolina and slashed .305/.418/.711 during his junior year. He has extremely quick and powerful hands that generate above-average pull power. Horvath is geared to pull in the extreme but so far his bat is quick enough to make this style of hitting work. It does leave Horvath vulnerable to breaking stuff down and away from him, but Horvath tends to identify them and doesn't often chase. He played third base early during his college career but wasn't very good there, and he's moved to the outfield. He doesn't run well enough to play center but he is fast enough, and plays with enough effort, to be a plus corner outfield defender with continued reps there. He projects as the short end of a corner platoon.

Anderson is a very physical second baseman with plus bat speed. He hit (this is not a typo) .414/.461/.771 as a junior and more than doubled his career home run total with 21 bombs. Why wasn't he a first rounder? His swing might not play in pro ball. Anderson is great at identifying and barreling low pitches but his path is often underneath stuff at the letters. He's often bent at the waist and spraying contact to the opposite field with his bottom-hand-dominant swing, and rarely pulls the ball. When he connects, Anderson puts a huge charge into the baseball, it's just possible he won't connect enough in pro ball. He's seen action all over the infield and is fine at both second and third base. Even if he's flawed as a contact hitter, so long as Anderson can play two infield spots, he has enough power to carry a part time infield profile.

Ultra-deceptive cross-bodied lefty with a rise/run heater. Stride direction takes him toward the first base line at an extreme angle, and this in concert with Sullivan's low three-quarters slot makes him very deceptive, it takes hitters a few looks at him to get comfortable. Does most of his swing-and-miss damage with a low-90s fastball that averaged 90 mph across all of 2023 but was sitting more 90-94 during his postseason starts. Fastball-heavy approach in the extreme at about 75% usage, which isn't sustainable in pro ball. Slider length helps the 77-81 mph pitch play left-on-left, changeup (80-84 mph) often has slider look due to angle. There aren't any big league starters who look like this, more likely Sullivan is a low-leverage long man or second lefty coming out of the bullpen.

Keener moved back and forth between the bullpen and rotation as a sophomore and junior, and it's plausible that some of his current issues (changeup quality and consistency, overall command) have late projection due to lack of reps, while some of his other issues (fastball shape and quality dragging down his mid-90s fastball) need more significant dev intervention. There's an impact slider here, a nasty two-plane sweeper in the mid-80s. There are two potential impact pitches in the fastball and slider if Keener is just airing it out in single-inning relief. He should be developed as a starter with hope the changeup feel comes and that his fastball movement can be improved, but Wake tends not to leave a lot of meat on the bone, especially as far as fastball effectiveness is concerned. Keener is likely a standard middle reliever, a fourth round prospect.

Arizona's "ace" has relief projection in pro ball. Nichols throws really hard (routinely 94-97 mph) but with ineffectual shape and often with reliever's fastball command. A three-pitch mix headlined by the fastball and a mid-80s slider perhaps gives him a shot to start, but Nichols barely used his changeup in college and, developmentally, is a two-pitch guy right now. Glove-side command of the upper-80s slider is much more consistent than his fastball feel. He should be developed as a starter in pro ball but probably needs more velo for the fastball to play above average, which is more likely to come in relief.

Witt had late-first and comp round homes during his high school draft year, but teams wouldn't meet his asking price and he ended up at Texas, where he mostly pitched in a multi-inning, high-leverage relief role as a freshman, which continued on Cape Cod and with Team USA. Put in Texas' rotation as a sophomore, Witt made just two starts before his elbow blew out, which required Tommy John. He was back toward the end of the 2023 collegiate season and didn't look very good, only sitting 90 mph with scattered command. Breaking ball depth and changeup sink are still there. He's a from-scratch pro dev project who needs a delivery overhaul — this tall, cross-bodied thing he's doing post-op makes his fastball steep and very hittable. He would be a 35+ FV prospect free of context, but that breaking ball is still in there, so he gets a little bump.

From the many athletic Hackenbergs, Drue was a draft-eligible sophomore at Virginia Tech whose spring ERA was approaching 6.00. Hackenberg's sinker, which sits 93-94, tends to find barrels and he surrendered 113 hits in 85 innings as a soph. There are times when his sinker has late, nasty tail back over the plate, and Hackenberg's slider should theoretically play well off his fastball, which goes tailing in the oposite direction. Hackenberg's slider has sweeping action, and when he isn't locating it where it can get whiffs, he's locating it where it can be tagged. He threw his fastball and slider a combined 94% of the time in 2023, so a lot has to happen for Hackenberg to be a starter. He avoided walks in his two years at Tech but his delivery (the cadence of which disrupts hitters' timing) is atypical of a starter. He looks like a solid middle reliever.

Came to Florida State with a lot of profile and ran an ERA over 5.00. Draft-eligible soph, body has mostly matured, still has a lovely and athletic move down the mound with impressive flexibility in the lower half. Arm stroke is often late, head whack adds to relief risk. Flat, rising heater with plus life in the 92-94 range most of the time, up to 96. Mid-70s curveball has monster depth. No real performance track record to speak of here, bullpen risk because of the delivery and college walk rates, but still really interesting because of what his lower body is doing throughout his delivery, the traits on his fastball, and the natural snap his curveball has. A late-blooming college relief prospect.

Best has some of the most exciting physical projection in the 2023 class. He is built like an NFL wide receiver prospect and his low-ball swing is geared for lift, enabling him to hit some epic pull-side shots. His swing is so uphill that he has a huge hole at the top of the zone, which is compounded by his lever length. A toolsy developmental project, Best's high-risk hit tool puts him in an FV tier of extreme risk and variance.

Baltimore's unsigned third rounder from 2022, McLean is a two-way prospect with plus power and arm strength as a third baseman. McLean brings mid-90s heat on the mound; the rest of his repertoire needs love from pro player development. He'll show you a low-90s cutter, a mid-80s slider, and an upper-70s curveball, all of which are inconsistent and tend to finish in the heart of the zone. But McLean is a special athlete with a special arm and he's barely pitched. He needs to refine at least one breaking ball to profile as a reliever.

Well-built, medium-framed righty with rock-and-fire delivery. Always works from the stretch. Open stride helps clear his front side and creates north/south arm slot. Near 12:00 axis on the fastball, at times has natural cut. Average athlete who needs effort to generate 90-94 mph fastball but throws strikes, just 27 walks in 105 innings in 2023. Slider is hard (at times 87 mph) for a guy who sits 92, shape varies but is mostly downward. Pairs nicely with the fastball. Creates bat-missing action on a low-80s changeup but struggles to find feel for location, which is common from arm slots like this. Up/down starter projection unless he can develop two distinct breakers as a pro.

If Rose can clean up his defensive shortcomings (mostly his arm — per Synergy, he only caught three of 24 would-be basestealers in 2022), he has a shot to be an everyday catcher thanks to his precocious feel to hit. Lauded for his makeup, it's fair to bet he will. Rose is a willing and mobile ball-blocker whose framing and receiving are fair, while his throws to the bag tend to be in the 2.00 to 2.05 range with mixed accuracy. His downward bat path enables him to get on top of high fastballs but it also causes him to drive the ball into the ground a ton. He has the frame and in-the-box athleticism to do more damage as he reaches physical maturity, but it might take a swing change to actualize. Even a one-dimensional offensive catcher is a boon at the big league level, and while you have to project heavily on several aspects of Rose's game for him to get there, based on this young man's attitude and athleticism, it's not all that out of reach.

Jones' combination of present baseball ability and physical projection are unmatched in the 2022 draft class. At age 14, thin as a rail, he already was hitting balls out of big league spring training stadiums during workouts. Now he's a strapping 6-foot-4 and has grown into considerable power, all while maintaining some amount of future physical projection (i.e. there is going to be more power here) and impact, up-the-middle defensive ability. While he's taken groundballs at shortstop in the past and is arguably athletic enough to develop there in pro ball, Jones is such a savant in center field that scouts won't typically entertain that notion, and he projects as a 70-grade center field. His first step can be a little delayed, but Jones' huge strides eat up tons of ground in the outfield, and he gallivants into the gaps, robs would-be doubles, and has runner-sniping arm. 
Jones' swing isn't quite dialed in. He tends to bar his front arm and load his hands high, which made it impossible for him to turn on velocity on the showcase circuit, when he was facing better, faster pitching than he did during varsity play. Over the course of two years worth of showcase play tracked by Synergy Sports, amounting to roughly 250 swings on tape, Jones never pulled a ball to the left of the left-center field gap, and all but about a dozen of his airborne balls in play were to right field. This is a little odd, but it might be remedied with an unobtrusive mechanical tweak. Everything else Jones shows you in the batter's box is exciting. He's a plus rotational athlete, his hands are exceptionally strong, he can drive his top hand through contact to punish pitches at the top of the zone and sometimes alter his footwork and the bend in his lower half to dip down and barrel low pitches. Even though his stride is relatively conservative, he is still generating so much force with his legs that his back foot will sometimes come completely off the ground as he's making contact, à la Bryce Harper. Nitpicking about his swing actualization is fine, because we're talking about the top player in this draft, but the foundation of present skills and tools, combined with Jones' physical projection, make him head-and-shoulders the best prospect in the 2022 draft and a potential franchise-altering superstar.

Holliday is one of the better rotational athletes in this draft, with one of the loosest, most beautiful swings in this class. He takes a big (but balanced) stride and can adjust barrel depth by getting deeper into his lower half through contact. He also has a good foundational feel for contact, and actually put balls in play at a better rate than most of the other high schoolers (including Termarr Johnson) did during showcase play, at roughly three balls in play for every swing and miss. Holliday's range, hands, actions and arm are all average, while his baseball instincts and internal clock are very good. He came out during his senior spring with much more raw power than he showed the previous summer. During his spring break, Holliday came to Arizona to work out and take BP with his high school team at some clubs' minor league complexes, and he (and his younger brother — you'll see him in a couple years) were putting balls out of big league backfields with ease. He checks literally every box, and there aren't many lefty-hitting shortstops with this kind of juice. He projects as an All-Star shortstop.

Our 36th-ranked draft prospect as a high schooler in 2019, Lee is a switch-hitting shortstop with above-average power, who walked nearly twice as often as he struck out as a junior. He was a coveted prospect as a prep player but his strong commitment to Cal Poly, where his dad coaches, and some general concerns about his physical longevity (due to a back issue) pushed the industry's assessment of him down, so he went to school. Knee and hamstring surgery effectively knocked him out for the 2020 season, then Lee hit .341/.384/.626 in 2021 and had a huge summer on Cape Cod, with six homers in just 21 games. He continued to play well as a junior, showing better barrel feel from the left side than he did as a sophomore. Lee has fantastic breaking ball recognition, and he can let pitches travel deep before deciding whether to swing. Even when he has to shorten up to protect, the strength in his hands enables him to do extra-base damage. He is much more adept at doing this from the left side, while his righty swing is relatively grooved. When Lee does take a comfortable hack, he shows you plus raw power, but his style of hitting is very balanced, and he doesn't sell out for huge pop all the time. 
This sort of offensive player would be a good everyday third baseman and a star shortstop. Lee played short at Poly, but based on his size (Brad Miller is a fair body comp), straight line speed (he's heavy-footed from home to first, in the 4.5s on my looks) and his medical, clubs tend to have him projected to third base. I'm a little more bullish about him staying at short, at least for a while, largely based on feel. He has quick actions, his lateral agility is better than his long speed on the bases, he's adept at positioning his body to be ready to throw as he fields the baseball, his transfer is quick, and his internal clock is well-calibrated. I can't account for what sort of long-term impact Lee's history of injury will have on his defense, and there's a pretty good chance his pro org will already have a more athletic defensive shortstop on their roster, but because his bat is likely to get him there so fast, he stands a chance to at least begin his big league career as a shortstop.

Johnson has the most electric bat speed in this draft, and presents a rare combination of present power and potential middle infield fit, while also being one of the younger prospects in the class. The stocky Johnson is short but not small, only 5-foot-8, but physical and explosive (especially in his lower half), and his swing bears a mechanical resemblance to Bryce Harper's, especially its finish. Johnson's size is actually an advantage for his swing, as he can enjoy a bat path geared for power and lift without it being too long. While especially adept at launching pitches on the inner third, Johnson also shows some ability to shorten up and cover the top of the strike zone. The outer edge of the plate is another matter. Most of his swings and misses over the last few years have been on fastballs running away from him, so while his short levers help him in one regard, they also impact his plate coverage in another. This may eventually require an adjustment. Johnson also has a tendency to expand the zone and make some sub-optimal contact, but there are times when he does this and impresses you with his ability to identify and adjust to hanging breaking balls, his barrel feel, and his hand-eye coordination. While his approach could use polish, Johnson also does lots of really exciting stuff you can't teach and is one of the most well-rounded hitters in the class, regardless of age. 
His ultimate defensive home is tough to project. He can make a lot of the routine shortstop plays and is likely to begin his pro career there, but his frame is already maxed out and he may end up physically developing in a manner akin to Chris Snelling or Willie Calhoun, which would hamper his ability to play any position later on. It's realistic to expect him to be a shift-enabled second baseman. Brandon Lowe's 2021 season is a great example of what the high-end outcome for a profile like Johnson's looks like, but if he can refine his approach, the ceiling on his hit tool (and overall output) is actually higher than Lowe's.

Neto had an incredible statistical 2021, then reinforced that performance by hitting on Cape Cod, and again by hitting (checks notes) .407/.514/.769 (!) as a junior. He's a compact-framed, contact-oriented middle infielder from a smaller conference, but Neto gets the most out of his body by taking one of the more athletic, high-octane swings in the entire draft. He has a cartoonish leg kick and his hands load similarly to Javier Báez, and while Neto doesn't have quite the same all-world whip as Báez, he is a plus rotational athlete who hits some epic pull-side homers. The huge swing doesn't detract from Neto's feel for contact, though he does dial down his footwork with two strikes and becomes even tougher to make swing and miss. He swung and missed just 10 times all year with two strikes on him. A plus athlete, Neto does some acrobatic things at shortstop and when he puts his whole body into a throw, he appears to have plenty of arm for the left side. He goes out of his way to try to throw while he's on the run, and while Neto's effort level is admirable, he rarely makes anything look easy the way big league shortstops tend to. He has a non-zero shot to stay at short, but I feel more comfortable projecting him to second base. There's enough hit/power combination for Neto to be a first-division regular at second base.

Parada was the rare high-profile California high schooler who left the state for college, traveling all the way to Atlanta for two years at Georgia Tech. He's a draft-eligible sophomore just shy of being 21, and somehow improved on an incredible freshman season (.318/.379/.550) by nearly tripling his home run total, walking as often as he K'd, and slashing .361/.453/.709 as a soph. Parada has impeccable hitter's timing, and batting stance aside, his swing is rhythmic and balanced. He has enough raw power to do damage to all-fields and Parada's feel to hit weaponizes it, as he often hits the ball where it's pitched, driving stuff on the outer edge to right field, pulling pitches on the inner third, and spraying everything in between. 
Parada is not a lock to catch. He is a fringe receiver and ball-blocker with a 45 arm. He is similar to Henry Davis and Kyle Schwarber, in that he may have to move out from behind the plate due to poor receiving, ball-blocking, and his raw arm strength, though he is pretty accurate. Whoever takes Parada will probably be a team that thinks he can catch. I'm less optimistic about that but it's worth trying, since catcher is at the very top of the defensive spectrum, and Parada's other seemingly viable positions are at or near the bottom (in my opinion, he runs well enough to play an outfield corner and I'm projecting him there, à la Schwarber's trajectory). Make no mistake, Parada's bat is one of the surer things in the draft, and he's likely to hit in the middle of a big league order regardless of position, which would make him a superstar catcher, but closer to an average regular if he ends up a DH.

The huge-framed Lesko has premium arm strength a dynamic changeup, and before he blew out and needed Tommy John during his draft spring, he was showing a much better curveball than he had in the past. He was already the consensus top high school pitcher in the draft before the curveball showed up, and would have been a top 10 lock had he stayed healthy throughout the spring, as Lesko is arguably the most complete high school pitcher to come along in the last decade or so. There were some arm action inconsistencies in the lead up to his injury that might be polished during his rehab. He's still arguably the best pitching prospect in the draft, even with the surgery, and poised to go in the middle of the first round at the latest.

Berry turned down seven figures coming out of high school and went to Arizona, where he raked as a freshman DH for a Wildcats team that made a deep postseason run. When LSU hired Jay Johnson away from Arizona, Berry was one of several players who transferred out of Tucson, following Johnson to Baton Rouge. He's draft-eligible sophomore in 2022 and a career .360/.450/.655 hitter, with his numbers improving in his sophomore year even though he faced SEC pitching. 
Berry has plus bat speed and raw power, with an uppercut bat path from both sides of the plate. His right-handed swing is pretty grooved, but still powerful, while his lefty swing is more skillful and dynamic, giving him a potent contact/power blend. Though he does his homer damage almost exclusively to his pull side, Berry slices breaking balls away from him to the opposite field, and most of his non-extra-base hits come that way. He can shorten up and punish inner-third velocity from the left side like few other hitters in the 2022 draft, and he rarely expands the zone. I have Berry projected as a DH. He's actually a fairly range-y third baseman, as his foot speed allows him to cover a lot of ground, but his hands and arm accuracy are both pretty rough, and cause him to be error-prone. Similar to Kevin Parada, Berry's bat makes him a stable prospect, but his lack of a defensive home caps his ceiling. He's similar to Dodgers prospect Michael Busch when he was coming out, and is one of the favorites to reach the big leagues first from this draft class, producing like an average everyday player even at DH.

Not since Bryce Harper has a prospect carved a path that has been optimized to appeal to draft models, in-person scouting looks, and (hopefully) in a very young eventual free agency. The son of 15-year pro Lou Collier, Cam is among the most physical high school prospects in the 2022 draft, even though he reclassified from the '23 group and will be just 17.6 on draft day. Like Harper, he got his GED, went to a junior college, and then (going beyond Harper) used the later timing of the draft to also play on Cape Cod. Despite being this size at this age, which might typically cause long-term 1B/DH projection, Collier's defensive feet, hands, actions, and arm strength are all excellent, and might make him a future plus third base defender. He has fair feel to hit, and has some raw strength as a result of his prodigious size, but the quality of his contact tends to be mixed (he gets jammed a lot), and Collier's swing path really only enables him to work middle-away, toward the opposite field gap. It's important to remember Collier's age when considering these finer points of hitting. He made a suitable amount of contact during showcase play, and presents teams with a solid hit/power foundation, though definitely with less physical projection than the typical teenager. Model-driven teams that don't contextualize physical projection are the ones most likely to be players for Collier.

Graham is one of the toolsier college prospects in the 2022 draft, and also the most projectable. He was an extremely skinny high school shortstop prospect whose shoulders have broadened in college, though he still has room for 30 or more pounds. Graham will show you impressive pull power even though he's rail-thin, and he has late-arriving power projection because of the way he's likely to add mass in pro ball. He is an incredible athlete for his size, playing low-to-the-ground defense and showing big league-level comfort backhanding balls in the hole, hosing guys with his plus-plus arm. After he looked lost at the plate early during his junior year, Graham righted the ship and was much better during conference play. His pitch recognition (especially against sliders) and bat control are not very good, and he tends to swing through a narrow band of the zone, not showing great tactile feel to hit. It's possible Graham will develop finer barrel control as he gets stronger and no longer has to incorporate his entire body to swing hard, but he looks likely to end up with a below-average hit tool. His defense and power projection are still impact attributes, and Graham stands a chance to produce an offensive line similar to that of Willy Adames.

The son of two-time Pro Bowl tight end Eric Green, Elijah became "Draft Famous" during his junior year, homering a couple times in high school tournaments held in big league parks, and looking much toolsier than all but a couple of the prospects who were a year older than him. He was seen a ton as a junior because he played at IMG, where lots of draft prospects from the 2021 class played, and played against. Scouts were blown away by his power and speed, but swing-and-miss issues were a concern. Green struck out in a third of his varsity at-bats in 2021, and swung and missed more than he put balls in play during that year's summer/fall showcase circuit (several other top high schoolers put two times as many balls in play as they swung at and missed; an extreme example is 2021 draftee James Triantos' 7:1 ratio) before things improved during his senior year of high school. 
What's causing the swing and miss? Green's swing is simple and direct, and he doesn't have an elaborate leg kick (he barely has a stride) or a complicated load; he just tends to swing inside fastballs on the outer third and expand the zone a little bit against fastballs up. He is as gifted as any player in this draft, a 70 runner with at least 70 raw power that plays to all fields. His long speed gives him a shot to stay in center field, but his routes to balls can be a bit of an adventure, and he's not a lock to stay there, especially if he slows down with age. If he even develops a 40-grade hit tool, then he'll hit 30 annual bombs, and it won't matter where he plays. There is hit-related bust risk here, but things trended in a favorable direction during Green's senior season.

Horton, who ranked 52nd in our draft rankings in the fall, had a breakout sophomore campaign (he's age-eligible) after returning from Tommy John, and he is arguably the best college pitcher in a draft that dealt with an unusual rate of attrition among that demographic. His slider took an especially huge leap and has become a plus offering in the mid-to-upper-80s, featuring two-plane wipe. Horton will also use a low-80s curveball with more vertical shape to both get ahead of hitters and finish them off. He also has nascent feel for changeup location, not often imparting bat-missing movement on the cambio but locating it in the right area. Considering how few reps Horton has had, that pitch (all his pitches, really) has an extra bit of projection. He very comfortably has the repertoire depth and command to start, it's just that he's only thrown 53 total innings in college and there is rightfully less confidence in Horton's durability than there would be had he been healthy and pitched two entire seasons looking like this. That risk is counterbalanced by the possibility that he's just scratching the surface in literally every other area.

Crawford has among the most extreme variance of players in this class. He played much less than his peers during the summer showcase circuit season and showed a couple of swing changes throughout the 2021 calendar year, making it harder to get a real grip on his swing. Things were more mechanically typical late in 2021 and in '22, and there's now increased confidence in Crawford's bat. He still has an abbreviated, helicopter-style finish similar to D-backs shortstop Geraldo Perdomo's left-handed swing, and he'll bend at the waist and throw his bottom hand at the ball to spray contact to all fields, but Crawford is adept at doing this with the fat part of the bat, and he surprises you with how much damage he can do with this style of hitting. He tracks pitches well, he can move the barrel around, he'll occasionally flash plus rotational explosiveness when he takes a max-effort swing, and his overall athleticism and physical projection make this contact/speed/present gap power package very exciting once you start anticipating that more strength will come. Though he didn't have quite the same showcase track record, Crawford's report reads a lot like a more-projectable Corbin Carroll's at the same stage.
